text:
Recent work supports modeling item transitions separately from textual similarity. [GaGNN (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2024.120623) combines group and individual transition graphs with sequential representations. [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) predicts complementary products through a directed, weighted graph projected from historical user–item interactions. These motivate an inexpensive graph signal alongside SASRec, although results on complementary-product benchmarks do not establish gains on this task’s next-item HR@10.

Relation semantics require caution. [KGSCL (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107191) uses explicit Amazon substitution/complementarity metadata to guide sequence augmentation; those relations are unavailable here. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines SASRec-style sequence modeling with BERT representations of titles, descriptions and reviews, reporting reviews as the strongest textual contributor. Its findings therefore do not establish the benefit of titles/descriptions encoded from scratch under the present constraints.

Practical inference: build directed transition counts exclusively from training histories; smooth sparse edges and account for destination popularity. Combine this signal with SASRec through a validation-tuned weight or gate. Encode available titles/descriptions using randomly initialized token embeddings and pooling, trained jointly on next-item prediction; separate source and destination projections allow asymmetric relations. Compare graph-only, text-only and combined additions using macro validation HR@10. Treat learned edges as predictive associations: purchase order and lexical overlap alone cannot reliably identify substitutes, complements or product compatibility. Keep unsupported compatibility claims uncertain.
